extracted.intended_audience: educated readers interested in literature and social reform (poets, critics, reformers, general public)
extracted.subtask_description: An extended essay-style prescription and critique describing what counts as Poetry (its nature, effects, and anti‑patterns) and what makes a genuine Reformer and social reform (aims, prerequisites, and practical evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhyme and metre not essential to Poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is not identical with rhyme, and measured rhythm (verse, metre) is not essential to Poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that 'Poetry is at least four thousand years old' while 'rhyme... can hardly be traced beyond the time of the Troubadours.' Examples: Chateaubriand wrote rarely in verse; Willis's finest poem 'Unwritten Music' is prose in structure. Use such examples to show that absence of rhyme or strict metre does not disqualify work as poetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as a mode of expression that elevates the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I understand by Poetry that mode of expression or averment which lifts the soul above the region of mere sense' — it reaches beyond merely physical/mechanical aspects to apprehend truth in its universal character and relations, so that natures are exalted and purified by its contemplation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the author's core definitional criterion: poetry must apprehend universal truth and produce moral/spiritual elevation. Examples contrasting prosaic statement vs poetic rendering (e.g., a plain assertion about Creation vs Job's whirlwind speech; a prosaic claim about creations of the mind vs Byron's lines) illustrate the greater vividness and force of poetic treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measured lines or typographical conventions do not constitute Poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere presence of measured and duly accented lines, each beginning with a capital letter, is not sufficient to make Poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit anti-pattern: formal verse conventions alone (capitalized line-beginnings, measured rhythm) may be mistaken for poetry, but without the elevating apprehension of universal truth they don't amount to Poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry achieves superior vividness and force compared to equivalent prose
rubrics_metrics.description: A poetic statement of a truth should carry 'immensely superior vividness and force' relative to a plain prose statement of the same idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct poetic passages (Job's speech, Byron, and the thunder/mountain passage) as models. Evaluate candidate texts by their intensity, vividness, and emotional/imagistic power over an equivalent prosaic claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic conception animates Nature as living and spiritually charged
rubrics_metrics.description: To the poetic conception, Nature is not a mere aggregation of matter but a living, conscious, vital universe 'quivering with deathless aspiration' because animated by the breath of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a thematic/imagistic criterion: poetry treats nature as animated and meaningful. Assess works by whether they present nature as vital and morally/spiritually significant rather than as inert matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's ethical and political vocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is essentially the friend of Virtue and Merit, the foe of Oppression and Wrong, the champion of Justice and Freedom; it cannot be suborned to the service of oppressive powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poem's moral stance matters: genuine poetry speaks against tyranny and oppression and supports justice; attempts to glorify despotism will result in feeble, unconvincing work (example: a bribed Dante would 'stammer out feeble, halting stanzas'). Evaluate poetry partly by its ethical integrity and resistance to being co-opted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's consolatory and inspirational role for the oppressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry brings hope and cheer to the patriot in exile, the slave in bondage, and the martyr; it assures that apparent triumphs of iniquity are temporary and that justice is ultimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the social effect of poetic utterance: does it comfort, inspire, and sustain faith in justice among the oppressed? This social function is part of what makes utterance poetic in the author's sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic technique: fusion of thought and imagery into 'glowing alembic of numbers'
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry fuses thought into heightened, musical language—transforming an idea (e.g., thunder echoed mountain to mountain) into an image and rhythmic line that amplifies its effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate technique by how well language condenses and transmutes thought into striking imagery and sound-patterns; the example lines given show how poets 'seize the thought' and transmute it into living language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reformer as Transformer—material transformation prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: A reformer (man as Transformer) must first change outward, material conditions; mental or moral development alone is insufficient when people lack basic sustenance and shelter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pioneer response is cited: one must provide for bodily needs (food, clothing, shelter) first so that higher pursuits become possible. Practical guidance: reforms aimed at moral instruction should be preceded or accompanied by material improvement—washing, clothing, and placing people in honest labor before expecting spiritual uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material/circumstantial reform precedes effective moral instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Showering precepts, tracts, and Bibles on squalid, filthy, destitute masses is ineffective; first remove them from degrading conditions, provide decent clothes and honest labor, then moral instruction may take hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an operational anti-pattern and prescriptive sequence: do not expect admonitions alone to alter lives; arrange for changes in circumstances first to avoid hypocrisy and superficial results.

rubrics_metrics.name: True reformer is a radical thinker who scrutinizes traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine reformer looks inward and forward: scrutinizes himself and all traditions, usages, beliefs, asking 'What is this for? What does it signify? If it were swept away, what would be really lost? Does it tend to the desiderated result?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character criterion: reformers must be morally prescient, willing to 'pave the world with eyes' that inquire, pierce, challenge, accuse, and arraign. They are often silent, unimpassioned thinkers whose ideas can set society seething.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-discipline and personal example as reformer trait
rubrics_metrics.description: The sincere reformer often begins with personal reform—examining habits, appetites, and luxuries (diet, drink, extravagance)—and may adopt strict measures (e.g., teetotalism) even if ridiculed as fanaticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reformers are expected to model the discipline they advocate; personal conduct functions as both internal purification and public example, though it risks caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interconnectedness of reforms and united opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Different reforms have sympathetic relationships and their enemies tend to unite across causes; opponents of reform will cooperate to resist change even when not directly affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic implication: understand reforms as mutually reinforcing; anticipate coalitions of resistance (example: a negro-trader aiding in mobbing a Temperance lecturer). Organize reform efforts with awareness of cross-cause solidarity and opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reformer should restore what has been taken (land, knowledge, privileges)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before condemning human nature, reformers may demand that those who monopolize land, knowledge, and privileges give back what they have taken so the people's capacities can be fairly tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy prescription: effecting reform may require restitution of appropriated resources and democratizing access to knowledge and privileges as a precondition for fair assessment of human capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social reform's primary aim: uplift the laboring class into partnership
rubrics_metrics.description: The great reform is the Social Reform: to lift the laboring class out of ignorance, inefficiency, dependence, and want, not out of labor itself, but into partnership and recognized mutual helpfulness with capital suppliers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define successful social reform by measurable outcomes: reduced dependence, improved efficiency and skill, access to fair recompense, and partnership structures rather than pauperizing charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society's duty to provide work and fair recompense for willing workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Society should be organized so that whoever is willing to work shall assuredly have work and fair recompense for doing it; the man who has only labor to barter is not a pauper by right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a normative standard for evaluating social arrangements and policies: prioritize employment opportunities, fair wages, and mechanisms that assure that laborers can convert exertion into subsistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communal/cooperative experiments as evidence of practicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples like the Shakers demonstrate that men and women can live and labor for general, not selfish, good: no paupers, no beggars, general thrift and plenty—evidence that cooperative social orders can succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical historical examples (Shakers) as evidence when judging the feasibility of cooperative or communal reforms. Success in some associations demonstrates capacity even if broader adoption is difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical caution about scope and material constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Many experiments have failed; the difficulty of creating and maintaining radically trustful social structures is often due to the character of the human materials available (those expelled by old machinery), so success in some forms does not guarantee universal applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate reform proposals with attention to human factors and context: failures do not disprove all alternatives, nor do successes guarantee easy scaling. Use analogies (a bank open to unlimited drawing would fail though a well‑managed joint-stock bank can succeed) to calibrate expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions and instruction shape human behavior; reform targets systems not only individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Reformers observe that men are better or worse as they have 'better or worse instructors, rulers, and institutions'—so reform must address institutions, rules, and education, not only individual moralizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both the institutional arrangements (laws, property, monopolies of knowledge) and educational/instructional regimes when diagnosing social ills. Effective reform aims to alter institutional incentives and access rather than merely admonishing individuals.
